Thursday, 17 April 2030. Julien is back from Paris, where he had a meeting at the Ministry of Culture with Catherine Dumas. In the evening he tells Ioana everything, in the kitchen.
Well? Tell me. What did she ask you?
First, she asked me if I had thought about her proposal. I said I had thought of nothing else for ten days.
She wanted to know what was making me hesitate. So I explained that I didn’t want to leave Lyon, or the La Duchère children, or you.
In that order? The children before me?
(laughs) I didn’t say in what order. Anyway. She asked me where I would like to work if I accepted. I answered: in Lyon.
She wondered for a moment whether it was possible. Then she said the ministry could open an office in Lyon, since it all started here.
And the La Duchère children? Did you ask them what they thought?
Not yet. But I asked her if I could keep the orchestra two days a week. She said yes, on condition that I find someone for the other days.
Do you already have an idea?
Théo. He’ll be eighteen next year. And I wonder if Lucia would agree to help him. She got the whole orchestra dancing in an hour.
And nobody asked me what I thought.
That’s why I bought you croissants. So: what do you think?
I think you’ve already decided. And I think it’s a good decision. But we’ll talk about it again at the seaside.
A question answered with yes/no becomes, in reported speech, a clause with “si” (if, whether). Inversion and “est-ce que” disappear:
Elle me demande si j’ai réfléchi.
Elle se demande si c’est possible.
Je me demande si elle accepterait.
“Si” + “il / ils” → “s’il / s’ils”. But there’s NO elision before “elle”: “si elle” (not “s’elle” ✗).
“Qu’est-ce qui” and “qu’est-ce que” in the direct question become “ce qui” and “ce que”:
Elle veut savoir ce qui me fait hésiter.
Elle veut savoir ce que je pense.
Elle demande ce que je veux.
Tip: if “ce” is followed directly by a verb, it’s “ce qui” (ce qui se passe). If it’s followed by a subject, it’s “ce que” (ce que JE pense).
She asked me where I would like to work.
He wants to know when I start.
I wonder how he’s going to manage.
A typical mistake: keeping the inversion. “Elle m’a demandé où voudrais-je travailler” ✗ → “où je voudrais travailler”. The word order is that of an affirmative sentence!

On Wednesday 23 April, at the end of the rehearsal, Julien asked the children to stay seated. He explained the ministry’s proposal to them in simple words: ten orchestras in ten cities, an office in Lyon, and himself travelling from time to time. Then he asked them what they thought. He expected cries of joy. There was a long silence.

Inès was the first to raise her hand. She wanted to know if he was going to leave them. Julien answered no, that he would keep the orchestra two days a week. She asked which days. He said Wednesdays and Saturdays. She thought about it, then asked who would come on the other days. Julien realised she had already done all the calculations.

Yanis, for his part, asked whether the other orchestras would also play Henri’s waltz. Julien said he didn’t know yet. Yanis frowned. “They have to play it,” he declared. “Otherwise it’s not the same project.” Several children agreed noisily. Julien wrote the remark in his notebook. He wondered whether a ministry could understand that kind of argument.

A little violinist in the second row asked, very seriously, whether Julien would become famous and whether he’d be on television every evening. A boy wanted to know how much he would earn. Another asked if he would have a car with a driver. Julien laughed and answered that he would keep taking the bus, like everyone else. The children looked disappointed.

Sami didn’t ask anything. He took out a sheet of paper and a pencil and drew. When the rehearsal was over, he came and gave his drawing to Julien. It showed ten little houses, each with a window in the roof. And above all the houses, a single musical note, very big, like a sun. Julien looked at it for a long time. He put it in his pocket.

The next day, Julien went to see Théo at the Conservatoire. He found him in a small room, working on a Beethoven sonata. He waited for the end of the movement, then asked him, without preamble, whether he would agree to conduct the La Duchère orchestra three days a week, from September. Théo dropped his score.

“Me?” he asked. “But I’m seventeen!” Julien reminded him that he would be eighteen in September, that he knew all the children and that all the children adored him. He also reminded him that at twelve he had played Henri’s waltz at Julien and Ioana’s wedding in front of a hundred people, without a single wrong note. Théo turned bright red.

Then he asked the question Julien was waiting for. He wanted to know if he would be alone. Julien answered no: he intended to ask Lucia to work with him. Lucia would take care of rhythm, dance, joy. Théo would take care of the music. And Julien would come on Wednesdays and Saturdays to check that nobody had got lost along the way.

That same evening, Théo’s mother phoned Julien. She wanted to know if it was serious. She asked how her son could prepare for the bac and conduct an orchestra at the same time. She asked who would pay him, how much, and whether he would still have time to sleep. Julien answered all the questions, patiently, for forty minutes.

At the end she sighed. “You know, Mr Moreau,” she said, “when I registered your daughter’s birth at the town hall, I had no idea my son would end up conducting her orchestra.” Julien laughed. He had forgotten that she was the one who had prepared their wedding at the town hall, then registered Rose-Hélène. Lyon really was a very small city.

Lucia, on the other hand, didn’t hesitate for a second. When Julien asked her if she would like to work with Théo, she only asked whether she would be paid. Julien said yes, thanks to the ministry. She asked how much. Julien named a figure. She thought for three seconds. “For that price,” she said, “I’ll teach them flamenco too.”

Then she added, more seriously: “But not before the wedding. The wedding first. And the honeymoon. I don’t even know yet where Radu is taking me. I’ve asked him a hundred times. He always answers that it’s a surprise.” Julien knew where Radu was taking her. He had sworn not to say anything. He changed the subject very quickly.

Odile had her questions too. She waited for Julien on the landing one evening, in her dressing gown. She wanted to know if each of the ten orchestras would have a hall. Julien said he hoped so. She asked if there would be a lime tree in front of each hall. Julien hadn’t thought of that. Odile explained that Mr Fournier, the gardener at the Tête d’Or, still had twelve little lime trees grown from Henri and Hélène’s tree.

“Ten cities, ten lime trees,” she said. “There’ll be two left. One for Paris, just in case. And one for Corsica, because you never know.” Julien looked at her in wonder. He wondered how a seventy-nine-year-old woman could have better ideas than an entire ministry. He wrote the proposal in his notebook, just below Yanis’s.

At home, someone else was asking questions, but only one, always the same. For a few days, Rose-Hélène had discovered the word “why”. Why is the cat sleeping? Why the moon? Why is Daddy leaving? Julien tried to answer every time, seriously, as if it were a real question. Ioana, for her part, had found a universal answer: “Because that’s how it is.” Rose-Hélène was never satisfied.

On Friday, Julien called Catherine Dumas. He explained his conditions: the office in Lyon, two days a week at La Duchère, Théo and Lucia for the rest. She listened without interrupting. Then she asked whether he would accept a trial year. If all went well, the contract would be extended. If it all went badly, he would go back to the Conservatoire.

Julien asked for a few days to think. Catherine Dumas said she understood, and asked when he could give her his answer. He looked at the kitchen calendar, where “15 May. Sea.” was written. He answered: on 20 May. She didn’t ask why. After hanging up, he wondered whether she had guessed.

Meanwhile, Ioana had other questions to deal with, questions that came from Iași. Her grandmother had been calling her every evening for a week, always at the same time, during the TV news, and every evening she had a new question. Ioana ended up writing them down in a notebook, to be sure she didn’t forget anything.

On Monday, the grandmother asked whether there would be sarmale at the wedding. Ioana answered that the dinner would be Spanish and French. The grandmother was silent for a long time, then asked whether she could bring some, just a few, for the Romanians. Ioana asked how many. The grandmother answered: “Two hundred. Maybe three hundred.”

On Tuesday, she asked whether French customs would take her jars again, as they had taken Radu’s in Corsica three years earlier. Ioana explained that it was different, that on a coach there was no check on arrival. The grandmother asked whether Ioana was sure. Ioana said yes. The grandmother said she would hide the jars under the blankets anyway.

On Wednesday, she wanted to know whether Lucia’s grandmother spoke Romanian. Ioana said no, she spoke Spanish. The grandmother asked how they were going to talk to each other, then. Ioana replied that they would understand each other with their hands, as she had with Hélène. The grandmother approved: “Hands are the best language. And cooking.”

On Thursday it was Elena who called. She wanted to know if Dan could make a speech in French at the wedding. He practised every evening in front of the mirror, with his old textbook from the eighties. Ioana asked how long the speech lasted. Elena answered: “Twelve minutes.” Ioana closed her eyes. She asked her mother whether it could be cut to two.

From Seville, the questions came via Lucia. Doña Carmen wanted to know whether there would be a window next to her seat on the plane, so she could pray while looking at the clouds. She also asked whether there was a church in Lyon where Mass was said in Spanish on Sundays. Don Manuel, for his part, asked only one thing: where he could tune his guitar after the flight.

Radu, in the middle of all this, no longer asked any questions. He had dark circles under his eyes, ate standing up and talked to himself walking down the street. One evening Ioana found him at the office at ten, redoing the wedding seating plan for the third time. She asked him if he had had dinner. He answered that he no longer knew.

The problem, he explained, was table number four. He had to seat the grandmother, doña Carmen, Odile and Mrs Roux there. Four women who were over three hundred and twenty years old between them and didn’t speak the same language. He wondered whether it was a good idea or a disaster. Ioana looked at the plan. “It’s the best table at the wedding,” she said.

On Tuesday 29 April, at six in the morning, Costel’s coach left Iași. The grandmother was sitting right behind him, in her usual seat, with two suitcases, three bags and a cool box which contained, according to her, “only a few little things”. She called Ioana before the coach had even left the city. She wanted to know if the weather was nice in Lyon.

After that she called every three hours. At the Hungarian border, she asked if Radu had eaten. In Budapest, she asked if Lucia knew how to make mămăligă. In Austria, she asked if the French mountains were as beautiful as the Carpathians. Ioana answered every time, patiently, even at three in the morning, when the phone rang on the bedside table.

On Wednesday evening, around eleven, Costel himself called. He wanted to know whether someone would come to fetch the grandmother at the Perrache coach station, because he couldn’t leave her alone with her luggage. He added, lowering his voice, that the cool box weighed at least thirty kilos and that he wasn’t asking what was inside.

Radu and Ioana went to Perrache together, at one in the morning, in Karim’s car. It was chilly. The street lamps lit the empty car park. When the coach finally arrived, they immediately saw the grandmother, pressed against the window, waving at them. She got off first, before Costel had even fully opened the door.

She hugged Radu, then Ioana, then Radu again. She looked her grandson up and down, as if to check that everything was still in place. Then she asked the question. Not in Romanian, but in French, with a terrible accent, a question she had obviously been practising for two thousand kilometres: “Tu as mangé ?”

Radu burst out laughing, and then, without understanding why, he started to cry. All the tiredness of the last weeks came out at once, there, in the Perrache car park, at one in the morning. The grandmother asked no other question. She held him close, as when he was five, and waited for him to calm down.

Costel unloaded the luggage in silence. When he lifted the cool box, he grimaced, but he asked no questions. He just shook Radu’s hand, very hard, and told him in Romanian that he would be there on 4 May, in front of the town hall, in a suit. The grandmother had invited him to the wedding during the journey, somewhere between Vienna and Munich. She had forgotten to tell Radu.

On rue d’Austerlitz, at two in the morning, a light was still on on the first floor. Odile was waiting for them in her dressing gown, with a herbal tea and a plate of biscuits. The two old ladies looked at each other for a moment. Then they hugged like two sisters who hadn’t seen each other for a long time. They had no language in common. They didn’t need one.

In the car, heading back to the Croix-Rousse, she opened the cool box and handed him a sarma, still cold, wrapped in paper. Radu ate it in two bites. Ioana, at the wheel, watched them in the rear-view mirror. She wondered how three hundred sarmale had been able to cross Europe without a single customs officer asking a question. She decided not to ask.

Reading text: The interview with the children
Marc Delorme interviewed the orchestra children after Paris. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Ce que les enfants m’ont dit

A week after the Paris concert, I went to the Wednesday rehearsal with a notebook and a single idea: to ask the children what they had felt. I didn’t know if they would want to talk to me. They all talked to me at once.

I asked Yanis what had impressed him most. He answered without hesitating: “The metro.” I asked him if the Philharmonie hadn’t impressed him too. He thought about it and said: “Yes, it did. But in the metro there was a staircase that moved by itself, and it was broken.”

I asked Inès if she had been afraid. She looked at me as if my question were stupid. “Obviously. But Mr Moreau asked us to lie down on the floor, and after that it was better.” I asked her why. She shrugged: “Because on the floor you can’t fall.”

Sami, the youngest flautist, didn’t want to talk. I asked him if he wanted to draw instead. He made a drawing: a train, a big silver hall and, at the back, a man sitting on a chair in front of a door. I asked him who it was. He said a single word: “Daddy.”

At the end, I asked all the children what they wanted to do later. I heard “firefighter”, “footballer”, “vet”. But I also heard, seven times, “musician”. A year ago, according to Mr Moreau, nobody would have said it.

On my way out, I wondered what I would have answered at their age. I no longer remember. But I know what I answer today, at twenty-six: I would like to write true things. These children taught me how it’s done.
Qu’est-ce qui a le plus impressionné Yanis ?
Pourquoi Inès allait mieux par terre ?
Parce qu’on ne peut pas tomber
